name: Dataset Licensing and Provenance
blurb: What may lawfully be used for what, and how to tell.

points.desc: A dataset's licence covers the compilation; the underlying web text keeps its own copyrights. FineWeb ships under ODC-By while the crawled pages remain their authors' - which is exactly the distinction being litigated.
points.name: Licence and permission are different questions

points.desc: Whether training on copyrighted text is fair use is the live question in the AI copyright docket - NYT v. OpenAI, Authors Guild, Bartz v. Anthropic and the rest are tracked with current status on the lawsuit tracker.
points.name: The provenance disputes are on this site's own tracker

points.desc: The Stack gates access and runs an opt-out process for code authors; GPQA gates to keep benchmark answers out of training corpora. Access control is doing licence work that licences alone cannot.
points.name: Gating is provenance control

points.desc: Dolma ships a datasheet documenting sources, filtering, and decisions - the practice the field is converging on, and the reason fully documented corpora anchor this catalogue.
points.name: Documentation is the differentiator

reading.body:
A dataset licence and the actual permission to use its contents are two separate legal questions, and conflating them is the central risk in training-data sourcing right now.

The split across 17 catalogue entries makes this concrete. MIT and ODC-By together cover eight datasets, but a permissive licence on a compilation does not clear the underlying text, code, or other content the compilation contains. FineWeb is the clearest example: the compilation ships under ODC-By while the crawled pages retain their authors' copyrights. Six of the 17 entries carry licences in the "other" or "undeclared" categories, which means the permission question is not answered even at the compilation level, let alone for the underlying content. Apache-2.0, CC-BY-4.0, and CC-BY-SA-4.0 account for one entry each, so the field has not converged on any single instrument.

Where licences are insufficient, gating and documentation are doing the remaining work. The Stack uses access control and an opt-out process to manage the copyright status of code it cannot formally clear. Dolma publishes a datasheet that records sources, filtering choices, and provenance decisions, which is the practice that fully documented corpora are converging on. Neither mechanism resolves the underlying legal question, which remains open litigation across multiple cases tracked separately. What the data does not cover is how any of these licensing arrangements interact with compute procurement or power agreements, because the constraint here is legal and documentary, not physical infrastructure.
